title: MIP on a GPU: what cuOpt accelerates and why branch-and-bound stays on the CPU

blocks.text: 11.4.5 MIP on a GPU: What cuOpt Accelerates and Why Branch-and-Bound Stays on the CPU

The LPs of lesson 11.4.3 went faster on a GPU when they were large. GridCap's real product is not an LP, though: it is a capital plan, a MILP with yes-or-no decisions, and NVIDIA's cuOpt solves MILPs too. This lesson reads cuOpt's own log to see which parts of a MILP solve it runs on the GPU and which it leaves on the CPU, solves GridCap medium's capital-planning MILP with HiGHS on one thread and with cuOpt, and checks cuOpt's plans instead of trusting them, since lesson 11.4.4 found they do not repeat. GridCap is a fictional utility; its numbers are teaching data.
The Model
GridCap medium's start-year model, the same rows as lesson 11.4.1's LP with the shares made yes-or-no, built by `lps.gridcap_timing("medium", integer=True)`:

**Sets.** $`P`$ the 400 projects; $`Y`$ the years 2027 to 2036; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the years project $`i`$ may start in; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups.

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ started in year $`t`$ ($k); $`s_{i,t,y}`$, what project $`i`$ started in $`t`$ spends in year $`y`$ ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$ (887 variables).
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

428 rows and 2,387 nonzeros. Both solvers stop at a **relative gap** of $`10^{-3}`$: the plan is within 0.1% of the best bound the solver has proved (lesson 3.4.1). The target is loose so that the lesson's program runs in seconds.
Branch and Bound Is a Tree of Small, Dependent Steps

A MIP solver's work, from the lessons of section 3, has several parts: **presolve** shrinks the model (lesson 3.3.2); the **root LP** solves the relaxation; **cuts** tighten it (lesson 3.3.1); **primal heuristics** look for plans (lesson 3.3.3); and **branch and bound** splits the problem into a tree of nodes, solving an LP at each, until the bound and the best plan meet (lessons 3.2.1 to 3.2.3).

A node's LP differs from its parent's by one variable's bound, and the solver re-solves it from the parent's basis with dual simplex, a few pivots each (lesson 2.4.3 measured that kind of warm re-solve). Each node's LP is small; each pivot depends on the one before; which node comes next depends on what the last ones found. That is the opposite of the work lesson 11.4.1 put on a GPU: not one large matrix-vector product with thousands of independent rows, but many small sequential steps that each wait for the last. Thousands of GPU cores have nothing to do on one pivot.

So the parts of a MIP solve that suit a GPU are the ones made of large, regular, independent work: a first-order LP method on a big relaxation, and a heuristic that evaluates many candidate moves at once.
cuOpt's Log Says Which Parts Run on the GPU
`milp_gpu.py` keeps four kinds of lines from cuOpt's log (the worker drops every line that names the card, the CPU model or the memory). On the build machine, one run:
<!-- unverified -->

cuOpt's log, the lines that say where the work runs:
  Solving a problem with 428 constraints, 887 variables (887 integers), and 2387 nonzeros
  Papilo thread budget: 4 presolve + 15 CPUFJ + 1 GPUFJ + 0 structural within 20 threads
  Solving LP root relaxation in concurrent mode
  Root relaxation solution found in 153 iterations and 0.00s by Dual Simplex
Read with the full log of the toolchain's cuOpt probe, which shows the rest:

items: **Presolve** (Papilo, then cuOpt's own) runs on CPU threads: 4 of them here.

**The feasibility-jump heuristic**, a primal heuristic (lesson 3.3.3) that searches for a feasible plan by changing variables' values to shrink how much the rows are broken, runs as 15 CPU workers (`CPUFJ`) and **1 GPU worker** (`GPUFJ`). This is the GPU's main MILP job in the log: a search that tries many changes at once is the kind of large, regular work a GPU suits.

**The root LP** is solved concurrently: PDLP on the GPU races dual simplex and barrier (lesson 11.4.4). Here dual simplex won, in 153 iterations: on an LP this size, the CPU method finished first, as lesson 11.4.3 would predict.

**Cuts and branch and bound** run on the CPU, as do the other heuristics. cuOpt's documentation says the same in its own terms: with the GPU and CPU both running, the CPU works on the dual bound (the tree), and its `heuristics_only` setting keeps only the GPU's primal search.

blocks.text: So "MIP on a GPU" means: the GPU helps **find plans** and can solve a large root LP; **proving** a plan is good still happens in a branch-and-bound tree on the CPU.
HiGHS on One Thread Is the Plan of Record
HiGHS has no GPU MIP solver; its branch and bound runs on the CPU, and with one thread it repeats bit for bit (lesson 10.2.2). `milp_gpu.py` solves the model twice and checks the result:

GridCap medium, start-year model: 887 binaries x[i,t], 428 rows; relative gap target 1e-03
HiGHS, 1 thread: Optimal, objective 226,886, bound 227,074, 1 nodes; second run same bits: True
  check: violation 8e-15, integrality 8e-15, 8.28e-04 below the best bound: accepted

HiGHS stopped at the root node (`1 nodes`): its presolve, cuts and heuristics found a plan worth 226,886 and proved a bound of 227,074, within 0.083% of each other, before branching. The second run gave the same bits. That is what a plan of record needs: an auditor who reruns it gets the same plan, and lesson 11.4.4's manifest can hold it to every bit.
A MILP in a `HighsLp`: Integer Columns and the Sense

The first practice below builds its model as one `highspy.HighsLp`, the object lesson 11.4.3 introduced with `highs_lp.py`. The fields are the same as for an LP (`num_col_`, `num_row_`, `col_cost_`, `col_lower_` and `col_upper_`, `row_lower_` and `row_upper_` with `highspy.kHighsInf` for a missing side, and `a_matrix_` with `format_`, `start_`, `index_` and `value_`). For a row-wise matrix, `format_` is `highspy.MatrixFormat.kRowwise` and `start_[r]` is where row $`r`$'s entries begin in `index_` (their column numbers) and `value_`. Two more lines make it a maximising MILP:

if integer:                                         # leave integrality_ unset for an LP
        lp.integrality_ = [highspy.HighsVarType.kInteger, highspy.HighsVarType.kContinuous,
                           highspy.HighsVarType.kContinuous]
    lp.sense_ = highspy.ObjSense.kMaximize              # kMinimize for a minimisation
A binary variable is a `kInteger` column with bounds 0 and 1. On lesson 11.4.3's toy, the integer column gave an objective of 12 and the same model without `integrality_` gave 12.5.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A cuOpt Plan Is Checked, Not Trusted

cuOpt's plans do not repeat (in lesson 11.4.4, two runs with the same settings returned different plans), and its status may not say what a reader expects, so a program never takes its plan on its word. `check` tests three things against the model's own lists, not against anything cuOpt reported about itself:

def check(m: dict, run: dict, best_bound: float, gap: float = GAP) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Rows and bounds kept, every value integral, and the objective within `gap` of the best proven bound
    (a maximization: no plan is worth more than any solver's bound)."""
    x = run["x"]
    broken = violation(m, x)
    integral = max(abs(v - round(v)) for v in x)
    shortfall = (best_bound - run["objective"]) / abs(best_bound)
    ok = broken <= 1e-6 and integral <= 1e-5 and shortfall <= gap

items: **Feasible:** every row and bound kept, to $`10^{-6}`$.
**Integral:** every value within $`10^{-5}`$ of a whole number.

**Good enough:** the objective within the gap of the **best bound any solver proved**. For a maximisation each solver's bound is an upper limit on every plan, so the smallest of them is the tightest, and a plan is measured against that, not against the bound of the solver that found it.

blocks.text: On the build machine, cuOpt with the same gap target and a 60-second limit, twice:
<!-- unverified -->

HiGHS's two runs took 4.2 s and 4.2 s on one thread
best bound proved by any solver: 227,045
cuOpt run 1: FeasibleFound, objective 226,856, its bound 227,046, gap 8.4e-04, 76,961 nodes, 8.5 s
  check: violation 0e+00, integrality 0e+00, 8.32e-04 below the best bound: accepted
  starts that differ from HiGHS's plan: 34
cuOpt run 2: FeasibleFound, objective 226,819, its bound 227,045, gap 1.0e-03, 67,430 nodes, 7.2 s
  check: violation 0e+00, integrality 0e+00, 9.95e-04 below the best bound: accepted
  starts that differ from HiGHS's plan: 29
cuOpt's two plans the same: False, same bits: False
What the run shows:

items: **Both plans pass the check.** They keep every row, are integral, and are within 0.1% of the best bound, 227,045, which cuOpt's second run proved (tighter than HiGHS's 227,074).

**The two runs found different plans,** worth 226,856 and 226,819, after different trees (76,961 and 67,430 nodes) and times. Neither is the plan of record; each differs from HiGHS's in 29 to 34 start decisions, and all three are within the gap. This is what "optimal within 0.1%" allows: many plans, none promised. Earlier runs of the same program found plans worth 226,828, 226,830 and 226,923.

**The status is `FeasibleFound`, not `Optimal`,** although both runs stopped at the gap target well inside the time limit. Code that accepts only `Optimal` would discard both plans; code that accepts any `FeasibleFound` would also accept a plan stopped far from the gap. The check above decides from the numbers, not the label.

**The GPU did not make it faster here.** HiGHS reached the same gap at the root node in 4.2 seconds; cuOpt took 7.2 to 8.5 seconds and tens of thousands of nodes. On the toolchain's harder 300-binary MILP, cuOpt reached its gap in 14.6 and 30.0 seconds against HiGHS's 44. Measure on your own models (lesson 5.4.2).

blocks.text: The determinism setting `mip_determinism_mode` did not make cuOpt's plans repeat either (lesson 11.4.4): two 20-second runs on this model explored the same 127 nodes and returned plans worth 204,983 and 204,849, with a gap of 11%, both stopped by the clock.

So a cuOpt MILP plan has a place: a **starting plan** handed to HiGHS (lesson 11.2.1), or a quick plan for a what-if, always checked as above. The plan of record comes from the CPU solver that repeats.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **Branch and bound is a tree of small, dependent steps.** Node LPs are warm re-solves of a few pivots each; they do not spread over thousands of cores.
**cuOpt's log says which parts run on the GPU.** One GPU feasibility-jump worker and PDLP in the concurrent root LP; presolve, cuts, branch and bound and the other heuristics on the CPU.
**HiGHS on one thread is the plan of record.** It reached the 0.1% gap at the root and repeated bit for bit.
**A cuOpt plan is checked, not trusted.** Feasible, integral, within the gap of the best bound any solver proved; two runs gave two different plans of the same worth, reported as `FeasibleFound`.

Challenges

items: Hand cuOpt's plan to HiGHS as a start (lesson 11.2.1's `solution_hints`, or highspy's `setSolution`) and predict whether HiGHS's work to the 0.1% gap changes.
Set cuOpt's `mip_heuristics_only` to true and predict what happens to its bound and its gap.
Your manager reads "FeasibleFound" in the nightly report and asks whether the plan is good. Answer using the three checks.

blocks.text: Design Note: The Check Uses Every Bound, From Every Solver

A bound proved by any correct solver limits every plan, whichever solver found it. Taking the smallest bound across solvers makes the check stricter than any one solver's own gap, and it costs nothing: the bounds are already in the results. It also means a plan from a solver that reports a loose bound, or none, is still judged fairly.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change. Without a GPU, only the HiGHS part runs.

**milp_gpu.py.** GridCap medium's capital-planning MILP by HiGHS on one thread, twice, checked; on a GPU, by cuOpt twice and in its determinism mode twice, each checked against the best bound, with the log lines that place the work (*cuOpt's Log*, *HiGHS on One Thread*, *A cuOpt Plan Is Checked*). *Try:* Change `GAP` to `5e-4` and predict HiGHS's node count.
**highs_lp.py.** Lesson 11.4.3's three-variable toy in a `HighsLp`, with and without its integer column (*A MILP in a `HighsLp`*). *Try:* Make $`x_2`$ integer too and predict the plan.
